slides.title: Renewable energy has crossed the cost threshold
slides.subtitle: How falling generation costs changed the investment case — and what still has to be built.
slides.footer: Prepared for a general student audience | Sources on final slide
slides.notes: Open with the idea that the debate has moved from 'is it affordable?' to 'how fast can we deploy it?'.

slides.title: Solar PV is 90% cheaper than it was in 2010
slides.statLabel: Global weighted-average LCOE for newly commissioned utility-scale solar PV, 2010–2023 [2]
bullets: LCOE fell from USD 0.460/kWh to USD 0.044/kWh.
In 2023, solar PV was 56% below the fossil-fuel benchmark.
Onshore wind fell 70% over the same period.
slides.citation: Source: IRENA (2024), Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2023 [1][2]
slides.notes: Use the number as a hook, then explain that LCOE means lifetime cost per kilowatt-hour.

slides.title: Clean power now undercuts fossil generation
slides.takeaway: By 2023, new solar and on-site wind were well below the weighted-average fossil-fuel cost.
slides.citation: Source: IRENA (2024), executive summary, Tables S1–S2 [2]
slides.notes: Point out that 2010 solar is the baseline; the 2023 bars show the current comparison.

slides.quote: The economic argument has changed; the implementation work remains.
slides.attribution: Synthesis of the cited IRENA findings
slides.notes: Pause here. This is the pivot from 'why' to 'what now'.

slides.title: Start with one measurable action
bullets: Compare your own electricity rate with a local renewable offer.
Track one number: kWh, cost, or carbon — then repeat monthly.
Use public data, not marketing claims, to judge progress.
slides.callout: Costs fell faster than many forecasts. Deployment is the choice that remains.
slides.notes: Close with a single practical step rather than a broad slogan.
Sources slide. Keep visible during questions.
